newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Red Cross hands out food to disabled Afghan veterans.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross hands out food to disabled Afghan veterans.

text.p: The International Committee of the Red Cross distributed food and winter supplies on Wednesday to the families of hundreds of Afghans disabled by the country's long-running civil war.
"We are distributing food to 852 families where the main income-earner is disabled," said Jean-Pascal Salvaj, relief delegate for the ICRC.
"We provide support for 30,000 families -- about 180,000 people -- in Kabul, of whom 15,000 are disabled and 15,000 without a male income earner." said Salvaj.

Afghanistan has been embroiled in civil war for years, with the latest fighting -- between the Islamic Taleban militia and a coalition of armies including those of former military chief Ahmad Shah Masood -- taking place north of Kabul.
The ICRC co-ordinates its food and winter programmes with the United Nations, which focuses on impoverished families.
Mohammed Alam lost his left leg in fighting two years ago.
"I was on the front line when a rocket came in and blew off my leg," he said.
"I did not receive any money from the government or my commanders. I have not been able to work since."
Alam stood in line, propped up on a pair of crutches, awaiting his turn. His young son had come with him to help him with the sacks of food and coal.
On the back of Alam's hand an ICRC worker had written the number of his ration card in indelible ink -- a rudimentary measure to stop double-claiming.

The lines for men and women are separated. "We used to have a mixed crowd, but after dsicussions with the Taleban, they allowed us to continue to distribute to men and women on the same day, but now they have to be separated." said Salvaj.
The Taleban have declared the mixing of unrelated men and women un-Islamic.
Each of the aid recipients gets a distribution every two months, designed as a supplement rather than a sole supply of food.

"Each distribution is designed to provide about half the necessary calories for a family of six for two months." said Savaj. The United Nations estimates that each person requires 2,100 calories per day to survive in Afghanistan.
According to the ICRC, a survey held in August showed increasing signs of long-term chronic malnutrition.
"The nutritional situation is still deteriorating in Kabul." said the ICRC's Stoecklin. "It is the result of the war and the blockade that was imposed on the city before the Taleban arrived."
Ismael Omer of the United Nations World food Programme says that the availability of food is not the real problem.
"Food is abundant in Kabul, but not affordable to everybody," he told Reuters.
Stoecklin says that even wage-earning government employees are being forced to sell their possessions to buy food.
"Even government employees, who used to be among the better off in Kabul are having to sell things to buy food," said Stoecklin.
In addition to flour, rice, vegetable oil and beans, the ICRC handed out blankets and coal to the disabled.
The distribution of the blankets and coal marks the beginning of the ICRC's winter programme, aimed at helping some of the most vulnerable of the city's population survive the bitter winter months.
